statement: About a given triangle to circumscribe a circle.
heath_proof: Let ABC be the given triangle; thus it is required to circumscribe a circle about the given triangle ABC. Let the straight lines AB, AC be bisected at the points D, E [I. 10], and from the points D, E let DF, EF be drawn at right angles to AB, AC; they will then meet within the triangle ABC, or on the straight line BC, or outside BC. First let them meet within at F, and let FB, FC, FA be joined. Then, since AD is equal to DB, and DF is common and at right angles, therefore the base AF is equal to the base FB. [I. 4] Similarly we can prove that CF is also equal to AF; so that FB is also equal to FC; therefore the three straight lines FA, FB, FC are equal to one another. Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FA, FB, FC will pass also through the remaining points, and the circle will have been circumscribed about the triangle ABC. Let it be circumscribed, as ABC. Next, let DF, EF meet on the straight line BC at F, as is the case in the second figure; and let AF be joined. Then, similarly, we shall prove that the point F is the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle ABC. Again, let DF, EF meet outside the triangle ABC at F, as is the case in the third figure, and let AF, BF, CF be joined. Then again, since AD is equal to DB, and DF is common and at right angles, therefore the base AF is equal to the base BF. [I. 4] Similarly we can prove that CF is also equal to AF; so that BF is also equal to FC; therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FA, FB, FC will pass also through the remaining points, and will have been circumscribed about the triangle ABC. Therefore about the given triangle a circle has been circumscribed.

**Statement:** About a given triangle to circumscribe a circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given triangle; it is required to circumscribe a circle about the triangle ABC. Bisect the side AB at the point D and the side AC at the point E (1.10), so that AD = DB and AE = EC.

**Step 2.** From the point D draw the straight line DG at right angles to AB, and from the point E draw the straight line EH at right angles to AC (1.11). Then every angle which DG makes with AB at D is a right angle, and every angle which EH makes with AC at E is a right angle (D1.10).

**Step 3.** The straight lines DG, EH, produced as far as necessary (P2), meet one another. For suppose that they do not meet. Then, lying in one plane and not meeting however far they are produced, they are parallel (D1.23). Now the straight line AB, produced if necessary (P2), meets EH; for otherwise AB would be parallel to EH (D1.23), and then AB and DG, being each parallel to the same straight line EH, would be parallel to one another (1.30), whereas they meet one another at D. Let AB meet EH at the point K. (K is not the point E, since E lies on AC between A and C and so is not on AB.)

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AB falls on the parallel straight lines DG, EH, the interior angles on the same side, the one at D and the one at K, are together equal to two right angles (1.29). The angle at D is a right angle (Step 2); hence the angle at K is a right angle (CN3); and since adjacent angles on a straight line are together equal to two right angles (1.13), all the angles at K are right angles (CN3). Therefore the straight line EH, falling on the two straight lines AB, AC, makes the interior angles on the same side, at K and at E, both right angles (Step 2), and so together equal to two right angles; consequently AB is parallel to AC (1.28). But AB and AC meet one another at A, which is impossible for parallel straight lines (D1.23). Therefore DG and EH meet; let them meet at the point F.

**Step 5.** Join FA, FB, FC (P1).

**Step 6.** In the triangles ADF, BDF, the side AD is equal to the side DB (Step 1), the side DF is common, and the angle ADF is equal to the angle BDF, since both are right angles (Step 2, P4). Therefore the two sides AD, DF are equal to the two sides BD, DF respectively, and they contain equal angles; hence the base FA is equal to the base FB (1.4). (Should the point F coincide with D, then FA, FB are the straight lines DA, DB themselves, which are equal by Step 1.)

**Step 7.** In the same way, in the triangles AEF, CEF, the side AE is equal to the side EC (Step 1), the side EF is common, and the angle AEF is equal to the angle CEF, both being right angles (Step 2, P4); therefore the base FA is equal to the base FC (1.4). (Should F coincide with E, then FA, FC are the straight lines EA, EC themselves, which are equal by Step 1.)

**Step 8.** FB is equal to FA (Step 6) and FC is equal to FA (Step 7); therefore FB is also equal to FC (CN1), so that the three straight lines FA, FB, FC are equal to one another.

**Step 9.** With centre F and distance FA describe a circle (P3). Since FB and FC are each equal to FA, the straight lines FB, FC drawn from the centre F reach the circumference, and the circle passes through the points B and C as well as through A (D1.15). The circumference of this circle therefore passes through each of the angles A, B, C of the triangle ABC; hence the circle is circumscribed about the triangle ABC (D4.6). Therefore about the given triangle ABC a circle has been circumscribed. Q.E.F.

Note on path: the point F may fall within the triangle, on the side BC, or outside the triangle, but Steps 5–9 nowhere depend on which of these occurs, so a single argument covers all three positions. The meeting of DG and EH (Steps 3–4) is established by showing they cannot be parallel, which avoids any case distinction on the shape of the triangle.
